Lesson Overview

In our last lesson, you explored the "Death and Recycling" phase of Creationeering — specifically how to classify your mousetrap car's materials and components at the end of their useful life. You learned why stewardship doesn't stop when a product stops working. Today, you take those ideas and do something every real engineer eventually has to do: communicate your vision to the people who matter.

This lesson is all about preparing for Parent Pitch Night. Think of your parents as investors or clients. You'll present your car's design and performance, and — just as importantly — your detailed plan for its end-of-life phase. This isn't just showing off what you built. It's demonstrating that you thought about the entire lifecycle of your creation, from the first sketch all the way to responsible disposal.

Learning Objectives

Students will:

  • Explain the "Death and Recycling" phase of Creationeering as it applies to the mousetrap car project.
  • Develop a clear, concise presentation communicating the end-of-life plan for their mousetrap car to an audience.
  • Identify and articulate the objectives, constraints, and variables (OCV) considered in the "Death and Recycling" phase of their design.
  • Demonstrate an understanding of multiscale modeling by connecting macro-level end-of-life decisions to the atomic-level properties of materials.
  • Articulate a biblical perspective on stewardship as it relates to the responsible handling and disposition of materials in their engineering projects.

data.html:
A Call to Responsible Creation

Our Creator is the ultimate engineer — and the ultimate steward. Everything God made was intentional. He didn't just build the world and walk away; He designed systems that sustain, recycle, and renew. The water cycle, decomposition, the seasons — all of it reflects a Designer who thought carefully about what happens after something is used.

In Genesis 1:28, God gives humanity a responsibility: "Be fruitful, and multiply, and replenish the earth, and subdue it." That word replenish is key. It means to restore, to refill, to keep in good order. Dominion over creation isn't a license to waste — it's a call to manage wisely. That's exactly what the Death and Recycling phase of Creationeering asks you to do.

Tonight, when you stand up and pitch your mousetrap car project, you're not just presenting a vehicle. You're showing that you thought about your materials, your impact, and your responsibility as a designer — even after the race is over.

Genesis 1:28 (KJV): "And God blessed them, and God said unto them, Be fruitful, and multiply, and replenish the earth, and subdue it: and have dominion over the fish of the sea, and over the fowl of the air, and over every living thing that moveth upon the earth."

This mandate isn't about control — it's about care. As you present your lifecycle plan tonight, you're living out this verse in a very real way.

What Is a Pitch — and Why Does It Matter?

In the business world, a pitch is how an engineer or entrepreneur communicates their ideas to stakeholders. Think of the people who fund new products, build companies, or approve engineering contracts — they all need to be convinced that a design is worth investing in. Your pitch tonight works the same way.

Your parents are your stakeholders. They've invested time, resources, and encouragement into your project. They deserve to see not just the finished product, but the thinking behind it. A great pitch tells a story: here's the problem I was solving, here's how I solved it, and here's what happens next.

That "what happens next" piece — your Death and Recycling plan — is what makes your presentation stand out. Most people show what they built. You're going to show that you thought past the finish line.

data.html:
Building Your Pitch: What to Include

A strong engineering pitch covers the full story of your project. Here's what your Parent Pitch Night presentation should address:

1. Your Design and Performance

Start by briefly describing your mousetrap car. What were your objectives? What constraints did you work within — material limits, budget, size requirements? How did it perform? Share real results: distance traveled, consistency, any improvements you made along the way. Numbers are powerful. They show you tested and measured like a real engineer.

2. Your OCV for the Death and Recycling Phase

This is where you explain what happens to your car after it's done racing. Walk your audience through the objectives (what you want to achieve in end-of-life), the constraints (what limits your options), and the variables (what you can adjust). For example: Can the axles be reused in another project? Can the wooden frame be composted or repurposed? Does any part need special disposal?

3. Multiscale Thinking

Here's where you go deeper. Connect your macro-level decisions — "I'm recycling the metal springs" — to the atomic-level properties that make that choice smart. Metal springs are recyclable because metals have a crystalline atomic structure that can be melted and reformed without losing their core properties. That kind of thinking shows you understand why, not just what.

4. Your Stewardship Reflection

Close with the "why it matters" moment. Explain, in your own words, how this project connects to biblical stewardship. You've been entrusted with materials, time, and creativity. How did you honor that trust? This is the most personal — and often the most memorable — part of any pitch.

Presentation tip: Practice your pitch out loud at least twice before the event. Hearing yourself say the words helps you find the spots where you stumble or rush. Aim for 3–5 minutes — enough to cover everything without losing your audience.

Connecting the Whole Journey

Think back to where this project started — a mousetrap, some wood, a few wheels, and an idea. Since then, you've moved through the entire Creationeering process. You identified a problem, researched solutions, designed and built a prototype, tested it, iterated on your design, and now you're planning what happens when it's all over.

That full-circle thinking is rare. Most people only think about what a product does when it's new. Engineers who think about the whole lifecycle — including the end — are the ones who design things that truly honor the world they're working in.

Tonight is your moment to show that kind of thinking. Walk in confident. You've done the work. Now tell the story.

data.html: Common mistake: Don't skip the Death and Recycling section of your pitch to save time. That's the part that separates a good project from a great one. It shows your audience — and yourself — that you understand engineering is about more than just making something work.

data.title: Optional: Pitch Checklist
data.html:
Use this checklist as you prepare. You don't need to follow it word for word — it's just a guide to make sure you haven't missed anything important.

  • Briefly introduced your mousetrap car and its design goals
  • Shared at least one performance result (distance, speed, consistency)
  • Described the objectives, constraints, and variables of your Death and Recycling plan
  • Connected at least one material decision to its atomic or molecular properties
  • Explained what will be reused, repurposed, recycled, or responsibly disposed of
  • Shared a personal reflection on stewardship and why it matters to you
  • Practiced the presentation at least twice out loud
